newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore PM accused of "political" defamation move.
newsitem.headline: Singapore PM accused of "political" defamation move.

text.p: A top British lawyer accused Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong on Tuesday of using the courts as a tool to get an opposition leader out of parliament.

Cross-examining Goh on the second day of a defamation case against Workers' Party leader Joshua Jeyaretnam, libel lawyer George Carman suggested to a packed High Court that the action was designed to bankrupt Jeyaretnam.
Bankrupts are barred from being members of Singapore's parliament.
"One way of making a member of parliament bankrupt ...is to use the heavy artillery of multiple actions to obtain massive damages," he said. "Is that part of your strategy?"
When Goh said it was not, Carman added:

"You and your 10 political colleagues saw this as a method of causing financial oppression on this 71-year-old man because you wanted him out of parliament and thought the court would provide a convenient method."
"No. Mr Jeyaretnam is not a threat to the PAP," responded Goh in reference to his ruling People's Action Party (PAP), which has run Singapore since it became self-governing in 1959.
Goh, his predecessor, Lee Kuan Yew, and nine other PAP leaders accused Jeyaretnam of defaming them at a last rally before January 2 elections.
Jeyaratnem told the rally that a fellow opposition candidate had filed police reports against the PAP leaders accusing them of lying.
The PAP swept back to power at the polls, taking 81 of the 83 seats in parliament.
The trial is being monitored by international human rights bodies, including the Geneva-based International Commission of Jurists and Amnesty International.

"Amnesty International is concerned at reports that the Government of Singapore has used civil defamation suits against political opponents in a manner that violates their right to freely hold and peacefully express their convictions," the London-based organisation said in a statement.
The PAP leadership denies using the courts to silence the opposition. It is a question, Goh has said, of challenging allegations that would undermine his ability to govern.

The case against Jeyaretnam is the second this year against a Workers' Party member. As in the first, the allegations stem from an election campaign in which the PAP turned all its weapons on Tang Liang Hong.
They accused Tang of being "an anti-Christian, Chinese chauvinist" who endangered racial harmony in predominantly ethnic Chinese Singapore, which has substantial minorities of Malays and Tamils.
Goh and his colleagues sued Tang over a variety of comments, including the lying charge. Tang fled Singapore saying his life had been threatened and did not return to defend himself.
The cases were awarded to the PAP leaders. They won a record S$8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in damages and then sued Jeyaretnam, accusing him of endorsing Tang's charge of lying.
"Mr Tang Liang Hong has just placed before me two reports he has made to police against, you know, Mr Goh Chok Tong and his people," Jeyaretnam told the election rally.

Goh's counsel Tom Shields, another top London libel lawyer, said that comment amounted to an endorsement of Tang's charges, which had been widely publicised. No one in Singapore could have been unaware of them, he said.
But Carman said Jeyaretnam had not endorsed Tang's statements and questioned why the PAP had sued his client.
Was it because Jeyaretnam, a lawyer, had acted for Tang? Was it in any way connected to this? Carman asked.
"If you are suggesting that we took action because he appeared for Mr Tang, that is completely wrong," Goh said.
But Carman said Goh had filed an affadavit earlier arguing that Jeyaretnam's alleged defamation was motivated by malice because "of his conduct when he acted as counsel for Mr Tang".

"I really have to say you have not been truthful with the courtroom in the last five minutes," Carman told Goh, who denied the charge but conceded there was "a connection" between the suits and Jeyaretnam's defence of Tang.
